**Clinical Assessment: Cycle 2 Polyuria with Hyponatremia**

The main problem is progressive polyuria with worsening hyponatremia despite high urine osmolality and natriuresis during ICE salvage chemotherapy.

From cycle 2 day 0 to day 4, daily urine output rose from 1.40 to 9.75 L/day — an absolute increase of 8.35 L/day (596.4%). Serum sodium fell from 124.4 to 123.3 mEq/L while urine sodium remained elevated (241.8 then 196.2 mEq/L) and urine osmolality exceeded 540 mOsm/kg, indicating concentrated urine despite polyuria. Cisplatin and ifosfamide were stopped after day 3; etoposide continued day 4.

Established observations: polyuria magnitude, hyponatremia, inappropriate urine concentration (Uosm > Posm), and renal sodium wasting. Possible mechanisms include: (1) cisplatin/ifosfamide-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with partial response — but urine is concentrated; (2) desmopressin under-replacement or erratic absorption — yet Uosm is high; (3) cerebral/renal salt wasting with concurrent water retention — plausible given CNS history; (4) adrenal insufficiency despite hydrocortisone; (5) reset osmostat. The high Uosm argues against pure diabetes insipidus or osmotic diuresis.

Missing information critical for distinction: simultaneous serum osmolality, fluid balance records, volume-status examination, desmopressin dosing/timing, fractional urate excretion, and weight trend. These would clarify whether the driver is renal tubular toxicity, hormonal deficiency, or cerebral salt wasting and guide safe fluid/electrolyte management.
